lessons.title: Common Mistakes: Overtrading the Cycle and Chasing Late-Cycle Winners

body.text: The allocation framework from the last lesson is only as good as your discipline in applying it. The two most common ways investors wreck a genuinely good framework are trading it too often, and buying whatever has already won.

children.text: A cycle-aware framework doesn't fail because the ideas in it are wrong. It fails because of how people apply it: reacting to every data point as if it were a confirmed signal, or piling into whatever sector or asset just delivered the best headline return. Both mistakes have shown up already in this course's real examples, and both have a real, calculable cost.

markDefs.definition: A false signal that reverses shortly after you act on it, causing a loss on the switch itself, on top of whatever it cost to make the switch.

children.text: Chapter 1 established that phases are only confirmed after several quarters of data. Treat every wiggle in a single month's data as a confirmed phase change, and you will make far more portfolio switches than the framework actually calls for, many of them
. Each switch also has a direct, calculable tax cost in India that has nothing to do with whether your call was right.

body.caption: The tax cost of switching too soon, on a ₹1,00,000 equity gain

body.text: Selling the same ₹1,00,000 gain a few months too early costs an extra ₹7,500 in tax alone, purely from timing, before counting brokerage, securities transaction tax, or the bid-ask spread lost each time a position is turned over. An investor who reshuffles their portfolio every quarter chasing each new data point pays this drag repeatedly, and it applies whether the underlying phase call was even correct.

body.title: Calculate the Tax Drag
body.prompt: An investor realises a ₹2,50,000 equity gain after holding for only 8 months, well short of the 1-year mark. Compared to waiting until after 1 year, how much extra tax (in rupees) does selling early cost, using the rates in the table above?
body.explanation: Short-term tax: ₹2,50,000 × 20% = ₹50,000. Long-term tax: ₹2,50,000 × 12.5% = ₹31,250. Extra cost from selling early: ₹50,000 − ₹31,250 = ₹18,750, before brokerage or STT.

children.text: Chapter 1's opening lesson described a colleague who took out a personal loan to chase a four-year rally, extrapolating recent returns as if they would simply continue. Performance-chasing is the same mistake applied to sector or size choice instead of the overall market: buying whatever sector or fund has posted the best recent return, right when that run is most likely to be near its end rather than its beginning.

stats.label: ₹1,00,000 in Nifty Smallcap 100, CY2018
stats.context: The correction covered in Chapter 2, after several strong prior years

body.text: An investor who chased smallcaps into January 2018, after several strong years, and an investor who simply held the Nifty 50 through the same period, ended CY2018 roughly ₹30,000 apart on an identical starting amount. The smallcap chaser wasn't wrong that smallcaps had been a great trade, they were late to it, buying near the top of a run rather than near its start, exactly the recency bias Chapter 1 warned about, now costing real money.

body.title: The Hot Sector
body.scenario: A sector you don't currently hold has returned over 80% in the past twelve months and is all over financial media and social media. Its average P/E is now well above its 10-year historical average, and mutual fund inflows into that sector have hit record highs in the last two months.
body.prompt: Using what you've learned about performance chasing, what questions would you ask before adding this sector to your portfolio, and what would make you cautious rather than eager?
body.modelAnswer: The first question is where this sector sits in its own cycle right now, not where it has been. An 80% trailing return, a P/E well above its historical average, and record recent inflows are, together, the classic late-cycle signature covered across this course, closer to the signals that preceded the CY2018 smallcap correction and the 2022 new-age tech stock crash than to the start of a fresh opportunity. The caution isn't that the sector's story is necessarily wrong, it's that the market has likely already priced in a great deal of good news, leaving less room for further upside and more room for disappointment. Rather than buying the trailing return, the more disciplined move is to check whether the sector still fits the current cycle phase from the master allocation table, and if in doubt, size any new position smaller and add it gradually rather than chasing the headline number all at once.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: Which single change to how an investor implements the allocation framework does the most to reduce both overtrading costs and performance-chasing risk at once?
options: Switching the entire portfolio the moment any single data point changes
Using fresh money (new SIP or lump-sum inflows) to shift the portfolio toward the target tilt, rather than selling existing winners to fund every rebalance
Investing only in whatever sector had the best return last year
Avoiding all portfolio changes forever, regardless of the cycle
body.explanation: Directing new inflows toward the underweighted parts of the target allocation achieves the same tilt as selling and rebuying, without realising unnecessary short-term gains or reacting to every headline. It's a practical middle ground between overtrading and doing nothing at all.

columns.label: Fix for overtrading
points: Use rebalancing bands: only act when an allocation drifts meaningfully from target, not on every headline
Prefer directing fresh inflows toward underweighted assets over selling existing holdings
Wait for confirmation across more than one indicator before making a large switch

columns.label: Fix for performance chasing
points: Check current valuation (P/E, P/B) against its own historical average before adding to a big winner
Ask where in the cycle a hot sector's run started, not just how large it has been
Size new additions to a hot sector smaller, and build in gradually rather than all at once

body.text: These fixes reduce the frequency and size of mistakes, they don't eliminate them. A small, conviction-based tilt informed by genuine evidence is very different from wholesale flip-flopping between allocations every time a headline changes. The goal is fewer, better-reasoned moves, not zero moves.

cards.definition: A false signal that reverses shortly after being acted on, causing a loss on the switch itself.
Buying an asset primarily because of its strong recent return, often right as that run is nearing its end rather than its start.
Short-term and long-term capital gains tax on equity; in India, gains realised within 1 year are taxed at 20%, and gains after 1 year at 12.5% (rates as of the time of writing, subject to change).
A threshold, such as a 5-percentage-point drift from target, used to decide when a portfolio actually needs to be adjusted, rather than reacting to every market move.

body.text: Tax rates cited in this lesson reflect Indian equity capital gains rules at the time of writing and are subject to change; verify current rates before making any tax-related decision. Index returns are rounded and approximate, provided for education only. Nothing here is investment advice; consult a SEBI registered investment adviser or a qualified tax professional for advice on your own situation.

points: Overtrading the cycle adds real, calculable cost: switching a ₹1,00,000 gain from long-term to short-term tax treatment alone costs an extra ₹7,500, before brokerage and STT
Phases are confirmed only after several quarters of data, so treating every data point as a confirmed signal produces frequent whipsaws on top of the tax and transaction drag
Performance chasing is the same recency bias from Chapter 1's opening lesson, applied to sector or size choice: buying a hot sector after a big run, not before it
An investor who chased smallcaps into 2018 ended the year roughly ₹30,000 behind an investor who simply held the Nifty 50 on the same ₹1,00,000, a real cost of buying late in a run
Directing fresh inflows toward underweighted assets, rather than selling and rebuying, achieves the same tilt with less tax drag and less reaction to noise
Checking a hot sector's valuation against its own history, and sizing new additions smaller, helps separate genuine early-cycle opportunities from late-cycle chases
